claim_verdicts.evidence: Execution capture at stage-3: 'coredns-...-...   registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.12.1' twice for -l k8s-app=kube-dns; 'kubectl scale deployment coredns -n kube-system --replicas=0' -> 'deployment.apps/coredns scaled'. Matches versions.yaml coredns 1.12 (kind node image v1.34.11).
Capture: 'kube-dns   ClusterIP   10.96.0.10   <none>        53/UDP,53/TCP,9153/TCP' and 'nameserver 10.96.0.10' from the client Pod.
CoreDNS manual (server blocks): "This defaults to port 53 (the standard port for DNS)."

virtual-ips.md: "Each instance of kube-proxy watches the Kubernetes control plane for the addition and removal of Service and EndpointSlice objects. For each Service, kube-proxy calls appropriate APIs ... to configure the node to capture traffic to the Service's clusterIP and port, and redirect that traffic to one of the Service's endpoints". dns-custom-nameservers.md: "If you are running CoreDNS as a Deployment, it will typically be exposed as a Kubernetes Service with a static IP address."

"The CoreDNS Service is named kube-dns in the metadata.name field. The intent is to ensure greater interoperability with workloads that relied on the legacy kube-dns Service name to resolve addresses internal to the cluster."
Docs: "you can modify the ConfigMap for the CoreDNS Corefile"; default shown as ConfigMap name: coredns, namespace: kube-system, data key Corefile. Capture reads it with jsonpath '{.data.Corefile}'.

Manual: "Each Server Block starts with the zones the Server should be authoritative for"; root zone = "a server that is responsible for all zones below the root zone"; port defaults to 53, set with ':'; "Each Server Block specifies a number of plugins"; plugins with more options take a nested block in braces. Note the manual also allows directives on the same line (e.g. 'cache 30').

issues.text: Carried from round 1. Claim 11 is still unverified: no doc and no capture shows the coredns Deployment uses dnsPolicy Default, and kubectl was not permitted again. Round 2 added a sentence that rests on the same claim and promises the next lesson names the setting; the outline of k8s.l3.dns-search-and-ndots names dnsPolicy: Default but does not tie it to the CoreDNS Pods.
issues.quote: A setting on the CoreDNS Pods, named in the next lesson, does this; if their file named `kube-dns`, CoreDNS would send outside names back to itself.
issues.fix: Run the prompt 08 change in meta repo_changes_needed (show the coredns Deployment's dnsPolicy in coredns.sh, recapture) and cite it in claim 11; or rerun review 04 with cluster access. Until then keep the text, and make sure k8s.l3.dns-search-and-ndots states that the CoreDNS Pods use dnsPolicy: Default, or drop 'named in the next lesson'.

issues.quote: `forward . /etc/resolv.conf` sends it to the resolvers listed in the CoreDNS Pod's own `/etc/resolv.conf`, and the CoreDNS Pods are set up to receive the node's resolver settings there
issues.text: 'resolver' / 'resolvers of the node' / 'resolver settings' is not in known_vocab and not defined in Core concepts, yet it is where every outside name goes (diagram node N, title 'forwards the rest'). From the forward plugin entry I can guess it means 'another DNS server', but I am guessing.
issues.fix: Either replace 'resolvers' with 'DNS servers' throughout (node's DNS servers, DNS server settings), or add to the `forward` plugin line in Core concepts: 'the node's resolvers, the DNS servers the node itself asks'.

issues.quote: and the CoreDNS Pods are set up to receive the node's resolver settings there, not the cluster's.
issues.text: Every Pod's /etc/resolv.conf names kube-dns (prereq summary, section 1), yet the CoreDNS Pods' file holds the node's settings. 'are set up to' hides how and why; I cannot reconstruct why CoreDNS is the exception, or what would happen if it were not.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after 'not the cluster's' saying who sets this up (which setting on the CoreDNS Pods) and that otherwise CoreDNS would forward outside names back to kube-dns, i.e. to itself.

issues.quote: kind's Corefile has one server block, `.:53`, which takes every name on port 53.
issues.text: 'kind' is a tool name not in known_vocab and never explained in this lesson; I do not know whether it is the cluster, the installer, or a typo for 'this kind of'.
issues.fix: Replace "kind's Corefile" with "The Corefile on `donhang`" (or add a clause: 'kind, the tool that built the cluster donhang').

issues.quote: "Kubernetes writes a DNS record into a zone file whenever a Service is created."
issues.text: 'zone file' is not in known_vocab or Core concepts. The misconception (and quiz q1 d, q6 c) depends on it, so I cannot tell what belief is being corrected. Only quiz q1's explanation hints that classic DNS servers answer from it.
issues.fix: Rephrase without the term, e.g. 'Kubernetes writes a DNS record for each Service into a file the DNS server reads', and apply the same wording in quiz q1 d and q6 c.

issues.quote: Nobody edited a DNS record, and you only know that the cluster DNS sits behind the Service `kube-dns`.
issues.text: 'DNS record' is not in known_vocab; DNS is known only as 'translating names to IP addresses'. It recurs in sections 4, 5, 6 ('No record is written anywhere'), and the lesson's key contrast is 'answered from a watched copy, not from a record'.
issues.fix: Add half a sentence in section 2 or 3: 'a DNS record, a stored name-to-address entry a DNS server answers from'.

issues.quote: A lookup is a packet to that address on port 53, the DNS port
issues.text: 'packet' is not in known_vocab (TCP is known as 'bytes over a connection', not packets). I can guess, but the word is used as if known.
issues.fix: Replace 'A lookup is a packet to that address' with 'A lookup is a small message sent to that address'.

issues.quote: `wget` to one `echo-ip` Pod's address still prints that Pod's reply, because a connection to an address needs no lookup.
issues.text: 'wget' is a tool not in known_vocab. `getent hosts` gets a one-clause definition but `wget` does not, and its result is half of the scale-to-zero proof and of the Try-it expected result.
issues.fix: Add a clause: '`wget -qO-`, a command that sends an HTTP GET to a URL and prints the response body,'.

issues.quote: pod_ip=$(kubectl get pods -n network-lessons -l app=echo-ip -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.podIP}')
issues.text: The second block uses `echo-ip` (Service and Pods with label app=echo-ip, port 8080) and the output 'echo-ip-...-... saw ...', but the prose never says what echo-ip is. I do not know why its Pods answer HTTP or what 'saw' means. Quiz q3 adds `echo-ip-headless`, also unexplained.
issues.fix: Add one sentence before 'Then the script scales': '`echo-ip` is a Service in `network-lessons` whose Pods answer HTTP on port 8080 with their own name and the address they saw the call come from.'

issues.quote: A->>C: Services and EndpointSlices, kept up to date
issues.text: The diagram's first arrow is API server -> CoreDNS, but the prose describes the client -> kube-proxy -> CoreDNS path first and only mentions the watch in the third paragraph. Narrating top-down, I started with a step the prose has not reached.

issues.fix: Add a clause to 'The Service `kube-dns` has the cluster IP `10.96.0.10`': 'and port 53 twice, because DNS can travel over TCP or over UDP, another transport protocol'.

issues.text: 'trap' is a shell term not in known_vocab. The sentence says what it does, so I can follow, but I would not know where to look in the script.
issues.fix: Replace 'The `trap` near the top of the script' with 'A `trap` line near the top of the script, which runs a command when the script exits,'.

issues.quote: kind's Corefile has one server block, `.:53`, which takes every name on port 53.
